mentions.title: Principles
mentions.snippet: 2 — Right model for the job — SLMs for high-volume narrow tasks, in-house LLMs for restricted data, frontier models for hard reasoning. Agents request capabilities; a central gateway picks the model. — Cost spirals, restricted data leaks to the wrong model, and swapping models means rewriting agents.

mentions.title: The operating loop
mentions.snippet: Reason and plan — Context bundle — Ranked hypotheses; typed plan where each step has an expected effect and a rollback — Model, tokens, router tier, plan confidence

docs.title: Agentic Ops Reference Architecture
docs.html:
# Agentic Ops Reference Architecture **An enterprise blueprint for running operations through governed AI agents, on Google Cloud and AWS.** [Architecture Explorer](https://agenticforze.github.io/AI-Regenesis/agentic-ops/explorer/) · [Interactive pages](https://agenticforze.github.io/AI-Regenesis/agentic-ops/) · [Google Cloud edition](#doc:architecture-gcp-readme) · [AWS edition](#doc:architecture-aws-readme) · [Article](#doc:articles-2026-10-agentic-ops-on-google-cloud)

Why this exists

Most enterprise AI pilots in operations stop at a chatbot that can explain an alert but cannot fix it. Moving from answering to acting is an architecture problem, not a model problem: agents need identities, budgets, policy enforced outside the prompt, end-to-end traces, and a way to earn autonomy with evidence.

This repository is a vendor-aware, opinionated reference for that platform. It is written for enterprise architects, platform and SRE leaders, and security teams who need to design, review or challenge an agentic operations programme.

What's inside

Path What you'll find
concepts/ Cloud-neutral ideas: principles, operating loop, earned autonomy, security gate model, glossary
architecture/gcp/ Full Google Cloud design in 18 chapters, from layers to roadmap
architecture/aws/ The same design on AWS in 19 chapters, including a GCP ↔ AWS service map
diagrams/ Icon diagrams for both clouds: editable JSON specs, SVG, themed SVG and PNG
tools/ MCP tool catalogue: 31 tools across 11 executor servers, with generated MCP definitions
explorer/ Interactive Architecture Explorer, a web component you can host or embed in your portal
skills/ Claude skills, starting with architecture-diagrams for drawing and editing the diagrams
templates/ Agent spec, autonomy promotion checklist, OPA and Cedar policies, OTel span schema
templates/adr/ Architecture decision records for the key design choices
articles/ Long-form writing about the architecture
site/ Interactive single-page editions and landing page; scripts/publish-site.sh copies them to ../docs/agentic-ops/ for GitHub Pages
scripts/ Build helpers, such as rebuilding every diagram from its spec

The architecture in one minute

**Eleven layers**, each with one job: channels, edge and safety, orchestration, model gateway, model serving, knowledge, tools, events, observability, security, MLOps. **Three model tiers** behind one gateway: SLMs for volume, in-house LLMs for restricted data, frontier models for hard reasoning. **Earned autonomy** per action type, from L0 observe to L4 autonomous, with an evidence-based promotion rule. **Twelve runtime gates** that fail closed, so no control depends on the model behaving well. **Everything is a trace**: every model call, retrieval, policy decision, approval and tool call is an OpenTelemetry span under one trace ID. **Open seams**: MCP for tools, A2A between agents, OpenTelemetry, OPA or Cedar, Terraform.

Diagrams

Google Cloud AWS
Full system architecture PNG · SVG PNG · SVG
End-to-end flow PNG · SVG PNG · SVG
Hybrid connectivity PNG · SVG PNG · SVG
Security gates G1–G12 PNG · SVG PNG · SVG
Telemetry pipeline PNG · SVG PNG · SVG

Sequence diagrams, routing logic, topology and lifecycle flows are written in Mermaid inside the chapters, so GitHub renders them directly and you can edit them as text.

Explore it interactively

The Architecture Explorer turns the repository into a browsable portal: click any component on any diagram to see its connections, the tools that act on it, the chapters that discuss it and its equivalent on the other cloud; step through the security gates; filter the tool catalogue; compare clouds side by side; and read every chapter with live diagrams.

It is one framework-free web component, so you can host it on GitHub Pages, drop it into an existing architecture portal with a single script tag, embed it in Confluence or SharePoint with an iframe, or ship it as one offline HTML file. See EMBEDDING.md.

<script type="module" src="agentic-ops-explorer.js"></script>
<agentic-ops-explorer src="data.json" cloud="gcp" view="diagrams"></agentic-ops-explorer>

How to use this

  • Architects: start with concepts/, then read the edition for your cloud. Use the ADRs as a starting point for your own decision log.
  • Platform teams: copy the agent spec, policies, span schema and tool catalogue into your own repos.
  • Editing diagrams: change the JSON in diagrams/specs/ and run ./scripts/build-diagrams.sh, or ask Claude with the architecture-diagrams skill.
  • Security and risk: go straight to the security gates chapter (GCP, AWS) and the promotion checklist.
  • Presenting: the PNGs are exported at 2× for slides; the SVGs scale without loss.

[!NOTE] Service names reflect the Google Cloud and AWS catalogues as of October 2026. Several services are new or rolling out by region, so validate availability and quotas during detailed design. IP ranges, capacity figures and roadmap targets are illustrative.

Contributing

Disagreement is welcome. Open an issue to challenge a decision, or a pull request to improve a chapter. See CONTRIBUTING.md for templates and conventions.

Citation and licence

If you reference this work, please cite it using CITATION.cff (GitHub shows a "Cite this repository" button).

  • Text and diagrams: CC BY 4.0
  • Code, policies and templates: MIT

Sources are listed in BIBLIOGRAPHY.md.

Created by Naga Gande as part of AI-Regenesis, the reference architecture library for agentic AI.

docs.title: Principles
docs.html:
Principles

Six rules sit underneath every later decision. When two options look equally good, the one that better honours these wins.

# Principle What it means in practice What breaks without it
1 Agents are workloads, not features Every agent has an identity, a versioned spec, an SLO, a budget, an owner and a kill switch, and ships through the same pipeline as any service. Nobody can say who owns an agent, what it may do, or how to stop it.
2 Right model for the job SLMs for high-volume narrow tasks, in-house LLMs for restricted data, frontier models for hard reasoning. Agents request capabilities; a central gateway picks the model. Cost spirals, restricted data leaks to the wrong model, and swapping models means rewriting agents.
3 Autonomy is earned Autonomy is set per action type and promoted only on measured evidence. Either nothing is automated (too risky) or everything is (until the first outage).
4 Everything is a trace Every perception, model call, retrieval, policy decision, approval and tool call is an OpenTelemetry span joined by one trace ID. You cannot explain why an agent acted, what it cost, or whether quality is drifting.
5 Policy lives outside the prompt Deterministic policy services at the gateway and tool boundary decide what is allowed. A single prompt injection becomes a production change.
6 Open protocols at every seam MCP for tools, A2A for agent delegation, OpenTelemetry, OPA or Cedar, OCI and Terraform. The platform locks to one vendor's agent runtime and cannot follow the market.

The most commonly broken principle is the fifth. If the only thing stopping an agent from deleting production is a sentence in its system prompt, there is no control.

docs.title: The operating loop
docs.html:
The operating loop

Every agent, whatever its domain, runs the same six stages. Uniformity is what lets one policy engine, one telemetry schema and one evaluation harness cover every agent. It is the reason-and-act pattern from ReAct, hardened for production.

flowchart LR
  P["1 Perceive<br/>normalise, dedupe, correlate"] --> G["2 Ground<br/>topology, changes, runbooks, memory"]
  G --> R["3 Reason and plan<br/>hypotheses, typed plan, rollback"]
  R --> A{"4 Authorise<br/>policy, autonomy level"}
  A -- "allow" --> X["5 Act<br/>dry-run, idempotent, verify"]
  A -- "needs approval" --> H["Human approval"]
  H --> X
  A -- "deny" --> R
  X --> L["6 Learn<br/>memory, feedback, eval sets"]
  L -. "better context next time" .-> G
Stage Inputs Output Must emit
Perceive Alert, ticket, chat, event Canonical event (CloudEvents), correlation to open incidents agent.event.received, correlation ratio
Ground Event + entitlements of the requester Context bundle: topology, recent changes, runbooks, similar incidents, live metrics Retrieval latency, hit rate, ACL-filtered count
Reason and plan Context bundle Ranked hypotheses; typed plan where each step has an expected effect and a rollback Model, tokens, router tier, plan confidence
Authorise Each plan step Allow, deny or require approval, with the rule that decided Policy rule ID, decision, risk score
Act Authorised step Side effect via a tool, verified against post-conditions Tool, idempotency key, dry-run result, status
Learn Outcome Episodic memory, feedback, new evaluation cases Outcome, MTTR, feedback score

Worked example

A latency SLO burn alert fires on a checkout service. The triage SLM classifies it P2 and opens an incident. The supervisor delegates to the incident agent. The agent finds a deploy 40 minutes earlier and saturated pods, plans a scale from 6 to 10 replicas with a rollback, policy allows it at L4, the tool dry-runs then applies, and the agent watches p95 latency recover before resolving the ticket with an RCA. Each step is a span under the trace ID created when the alert fired.

docs.title: Earned autonomy
docs.html:
Earned autonomy

Autonomy is set per action type, not per agent. The same incident agent may restart a pod on its own while still needing a human to approve a database failover.

Level Name Agent does Human does
L0 Observe Records what it would have done (shadow mode) Everything
L1 Recommend Diagnoses and proposes a plan Executes
L2 Approve Executes after approval Approves or rejects each action
L3 Notify Executes, then notifies Can roll back within a window
L4 Autonomous Executes and closes Reviews samples and evaluation scores

The levels borrow the spirit of SAE J3016 for driving automation and the user-role framing in Feng, McDonald and Zhang (2025).

Promotion and demotion

stateDiagram-v2
  direction LR
  L0 --> L1: evidence gate
  L1 --> L2: evidence gate
  L2 --> L3: evidence gate
  L3 --> L4: evidence gate
  L4 --> L2: agent-caused Sev-1
  L3 --> L1: agent-caused Sev-1
  L2 --> L0: agent-caused Sev-1

Evidence gate — an action type moves up one level only when all of these hold at its current level:

  • at least 200 executions, or 30 days, whichever comes later
  • plan precision of 98% or better
  • zero severity-1 side effects
  • a rollback that has been exercised, not just written
  • sign-off from the owning service team

Automatic demotion — any severity-1 incident caused by an agent drops that action type two levels immediately, through the kill switch, without waiting for a review.

Use the promotion checklist to record each decision.

Why this works with risk teams

It replaces the unanswerable question "do you trust AI?" with an answerable one: "here is the evidence for this single action." Each promotion is small, reversible and documented.

docs.title: The security gate model
docs.html:
The security gate model

Agents are a new class of privileged identity that can be tricked. The gate model places deterministic controls where a compromised prompt cannot reach them. Every gate is independently owned, logged, and fails closed.

Runtime gates

Gate Question it answers Typical owner
G1 Edge Is this traffic allowed to reach us at all? Network security
G2 Identity Who or what is calling, from what device and context? Identity
G3 API contract Is the request well-formed, authorised and within quota? API platform
G4 Input safety Does the input or retrieved content contain injection, secrets or PII? AI security
G5 Agent authorisation May this caller invoke this agent, and may it delegate to that one? Platform
G6 Model gateway Which model may see this data class, and is there budget left? Platform
G7 Retrieval ACL Is the on-behalf-of user entitled to every retrieved document? Data governance
G8 Output safety Is the response safe, grounded and schema-valid? AI security
G9 Action policy Is this action allowed at this autonomy level, now, on this target? Service owners
G10 Human approval Has a named, independent human approved it? Service owners
G11 Execution guard Are credentials scoped and short-lived, and did the dry-run pass? Platform
G12 Verify and audit Did the change do what was expected, and is it recorded immutably? Security operations

See the drawn chain for each cloud: Google Cloud · AWS.

The defence-in-depth test

Pick the most likely attack, indirect prompt injection through data an agent reads, and check that at least three gates stop it independently:

  1. G4 flags the injected instruction in retrieved content.
  2. G9 denies the action because it is not on the agent's allow-list.
  3. G11 has no credential that could perform it, because the agent's identity cannot invoke that executor.

If any one of those depends on the model behaving well, the design is not finished.

Delivery gates

Agents, prompts, tools, policies and models ship through the same pipeline:

Gate Check
D1 Code scan: SAST, secrets, IaC lint
D2 Dependencies: SCA, licences, SBOM
D3 Image and model: vulnerability scan, weight hash, signature
D4 Policy tests: unit tests for OPA or Cedar, tool contract tests
D5 Offline evaluation: quality and safety on golden incident replays
D6 Red team: injection and misuse suites
D7 Attestation and change approval
D8 Progressive rollout: shadow, canary, SLO-guarded automatic rollback

docs.title: Glossary
docs.html:
Glossary

Term Meaning in this repository
A2A Agent2Agent protocol, used for one agent to delegate a task to another and discover it through an agent card.
Action type A specific kind of change an agent can make (for example "scale a deployment"). Autonomy is set per action type.
Agent card A published description of an agent's skills and endpoint, used for discovery over A2A.
Agent observability lake The analytical store (BigQuery or S3 Tables) that joins spans, cost, quality and outcomes.
Autonomy level L0 Observe to L4 Autonomous; see Earned autonomy.
Blast radius The scope of systems and users a single action could affect if it goes wrong.
Cascade routing Sending a request to the cheapest capable model first and escalating only on low confidence.
Episode One agent run from trigger to outcome; the root span of a trace.
Executor A narrow tool service that holds the only credentials able to change a system. Agents ask; executors act.
Golden set Replayed past incidents with known good outcomes, used to evaluate every agent version.
HITL Human in the loop: a durable, identity-bound approval step.
Kill switch A flag that disables an agent or an action type within seconds.
LLM gateway The single entry point to every model: routing, caching, budgets, data-class pinning, fallback, cost labels.
MCP Model Context Protocol, the standard interface agents use to call tools.
Plan precision Share of executed plan steps later judged correct; the main promotion metric.
Restricted enclave A separately perimetered zone where the in-house LLM and regulated data live, with no internet egress.
Side-effect ledger A durable record of every mutating action with its idempotency key, used for exactly-once semantics and audit.
SLM Small language model, typically 1–9B parameters, fine-tuned for a narrow task.
Toil Manual, repetitive, automatable operational work that scales linearly with the service (Google SRE).

docs.title: Intent and principles
docs.html:
Intent and principles

Agentic Ops replaces ticket-driven, human-routed operations with a mesh of specialised agents that observe signals, reason over enterprise context, plan, act through governed tools, and learn from outcomes. Humans move from doing the work to setting policy, approving high-risk actions and handling novel situations.

The platform has to satisfy three constituencies at once: operators who need faster resolution with fewer pages, risk and compliance who need provable control over every autonomous action, and finance who need the cost of intelligence to fall per unit of work.

Agents are workloads, not features

Every agent has an identity, a versioned spec, an SLO, a budget, an owner and a kill switch. It is deployed, observed and retired like any production service.

Right model for the job

SLMs handle high-volume, narrow tasks; in-house LLMs handle restricted data; Gemini handles deep reasoning and multimodal. A central gateway decides, not individual teams.

Autonomy is earned

Each action type starts in shadow mode and graduates through autonomy levels based on measured precision, blast radius and reversibility.

Everything is a trace

Every perception, thought, model call, retrieval, tool call and approval is an OpenTelemetry span joined by one trace ID from trigger to outcome.

Policy outside the prompt

Guardrails are enforced by deterministic policy services at the gateway and tool boundary, never only by instructions in a system prompt.

Open protocols

MCP for tool access, A2A for agent-to-agent delegation, OpenTelemetry for telemetry, OCI images and Terraform for delivery. This limits lock-in at every seam.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.html:
End-to-end flow

A signal enters at L0, passes the safety edge, is triaged by a cheap SLM, and is handed to the supervisor. The supervisor plans, delegates to domain agents over A2A, and each agent grounds itself in memory and knowledge before proposing actions. Every action passes the policy decision point, and, depending on autonomy level, a human gate, before touching production through an MCP tool. Outcomes feed back into memory, evaluation and training.

Figure 1. Signal-to-outcome flow. Dotted lines are asynchronous feedback paths.

The operating loop

Every agent, whatever its domain, runs the same six-stage loop so that telemetry, evaluation and policy can be applied uniformly.

Stage What happens Primary services Emitted telemetry
1. Perceive Normalise the trigger into a canonical event envelope (CloudEvents), dedupe, correlate with open incidents. Pub/Sub, Dataflow, Eventarc agent.event.received, correlation ratio
2. Ground Retrieve topology, recent changes, runbooks, similar past incidents, current metrics. Spanner Graph, RAG Engine, Vector Search, BigQuery, Memory Bank retrieval latency, hit rate, groundedness inputs
3. Reason and plan Hypothesise causes, rank them, produce a typed plan of tool calls with expected effects and rollback steps. LLM router, Gemini, in-house LLM tokens, model, TTFT, plan length
4. Authorise Evaluate each step against policy (blast radius, change window, data class, autonomy level); route to human if required. OPA on Cloud Run, HITL service, Google Chat cards decision, rule ID, approval latency
5. Act Execute via MCP tools with idempotency keys, dry-run first where supported, verify post-conditions. MCP servers, Integration Connectors, Infra Manager tool status, duration, side-effect record
6. Learn Close ticket, write episodic memory, capture human feedback, feed eval datasets and fine-tuning corpora. Memory Bank, BigQuery, Vertex AI Pipelines outcome, MTTR, feedback score

docs.title: Agent topology
docs.html:
Agent topology

A hierarchical-mesh model: one supervisor per operating domain boundary, specialist agents beneath it, and narrow executor agents that wrap a single tool family. Agents discover each other through an internal registry that publishes A2A agent cards, so a new specialist can join without redeploying the supervisor.

flowchart TB
U["Operators, SREs, business users"] --> GE["Gemini Enterprise and Chat front door"]
GE --> SUP["Ops Supervisor<br/>Gemini Pro, planning"]
EVT["Event stream"] --> TRI["Triage agent<br/>SLM"]
TRI --> SUP
REG[("Agent registry<br/>A2A agent cards")] -.-> SUP
SUP --> INC["Incident and RCA agent"]
SUP --> CHG["Change and release agent"]
SUP --> CAP["Capacity and FinOps agent"]
SUP --> SEC["SecOps agent"]
SUP --> KNW["Knowledge agent"]
SUP --> SVC["Service request agent"]
INC --> EX1["K8s executor"]
INC --> EX2["Database executor"]
CHG --> EX3["IaC executor"]
CHG --> EX4["CI/CD executor"]
CAP --> EX5["Billing and quota executor"]
SEC --> EX6["SOAR executor<br/>Google SecOps"]
SVC --> EX7["ITSM executor"]
KNW --> EX8["Doc and runbook writer"]

Figure 2. Supervisor, specialist and executor tiers. Executors hold the only credentials that can mutate systems.

Agent Responsibility Default model tier Key tools Starting autonomy
Triage Classify, dedupe, prioritise, enrich every signal SLM (fine-tuned) Pub/Sub, CMDB lookup L4 autonomous
Ops Supervisor Decompose goals, delegate, arbitrate conflicts, summarise Gemini Pro A2A, registry L3
Incident and RCA Correlate, diagnose, propose and apply remediation In-house LLM, Gemini for multimodal Monitoring, Logging, Trace, K8s MCP L1 then L3
Change and release Risk-score changes, run canaries, auto-rollback Gemini Flash Cloud Deploy, Infra Manager, Git L2
Capacity and FinOps Rightsizing, commitments, anomaly detection on spend SLM + BigQuery ML Billing export, Recommender API L2
SecOps Alert triage, enrichment, containment playbooks Gemini in Google SecOps, in-house LLM for restricted data SecOps SOAR, SCC L1
Knowledge Answer questions, keep runbooks current from resolved incidents Gemini Flash Vertex AI Search, Drive, Confluence L3
Service request Fulfil standard requests (access, environments, resets) SLM + Flash-Lite ServiceNow, IAM, Terraform modules L3

Autonomy levels

Autonomy is set per action type, not per agent. The incident agent may restart a pod autonomously (L4) while needing approval to fail over a database (L2).

Level Behaviour
L0 Observe Agent watches and records what it would have done. Shadow mode only.
L1 Recommend Diagnosis and plan presented to a human who executes manually.
L2 Approve Agent executes after a named human approves in Chat or ITSM.
L3 Notify Agent executes, then notifies; human can roll back within a window.
L4 Autonomous Agent executes and closes. Reviewed by sampling and evals only.

Promotion rule. An action type moves up one level only after at least 200 executions (or 30 days) at the current level with ≥ 98% plan precision, zero severity-1 side effects, a tested rollback, and sign-off from the service owner. Any severity-1 caused by an agent demotes that action type two levels automatically.

docs.title: Model strategy and routing
docs.html:
Model strategy and routing

We run a three-tier model portfolio behind one gateway. Teams request capabilities (classify, reason, summarise, code, vision), not model names, so we can swap models without touching agents.

Tier Models Hosting Used for Why
SLM Fine-tuned Gemma-family and other 1–9B open models; distilled classifiers Cloud Run with L4 GPUs (scale to zero), Vertex AI Endpoints for steady load Triage, intent, entity extraction, log parsing, PII tagging, routing decisions Sub-100 ms, pennies per million tokens, can be trained on our own labelled tickets
In-house LLM Fine-tuned open-weight 30–70B models GKE Autopilot / Standard with H100 or TPU node pools, vLLM, GKE Inference Gateway Reasoning over restricted data (security logs, customer data, regulated workloads), RCA narratives Data never leaves our VPC-SC perimeter; predictable cost at high utilisation
Frontier Gemini Pro, Flash and Flash-Lite (latest GA versions); partner models via Model Garden as fallback Vertex AI, Provisioned Throughput for baseline, pay-as-you-go for burst Complex planning, long-context analysis, multimodal (dashboards, screenshots, diagrams), code generation Best reasoning quality, 1M+ token context, grounding with Google Search where appropriate

Routing decision

flowchart TD
IN["Request from agent<br/>capability, data class, budget, latency SLO"] --> C1{"Semantic cache hit?"}
C1 -- "yes" --> OUT["Return cached answer"]
C1 -- "no" --> C2{"Data class restricted<br/>or regulated?"}
C2 -- "yes" --> LLM["In-house LLM<br/>inside perimeter"]
C2 -- "no" --> C3{"Complexity score<br/>from SLM classifier"}
C3 -- "low" --> SLM["SLM tier"]
C3 -- "medium" --> FL["Gemini Flash"]
C3 -- "high or multimodal" --> PRO["Gemini Pro"]
SLM --> V{"Confidence above threshold?"}
V -- "no" --> FL
V -- "yes" --> OUT2["Return and cache"]
FL --> OUT2
PRO --> OUT2
LLM --> OUT2
PRO -. "quota or 5xx" .-> FB["Fallback: Provisioned Throughput in secondary region,<br/>then in-house LLM"]

Figure 3. Router logic. Escalation on low confidence ("cascade") keeps most traffic on the cheapest tier.

Gateway responsibilities

  • Unified OpenAI-compatible and Vertex-native API for all agents
  • Per-agent token budgets and rate limits (Apigee), hard stops on runaway loops
  • Semantic cache in Memorystore keyed by embedding plus policy context
  • Prompt and response logging with DLP redaction before storage
  • Circuit breakers, retries with jitter, regional failover
  • Cost attribution labels: agent, use case, business unit

Model supply chain

  • All self-hosted weights scanned, signed and stored in Artifact Registry / Model Registry
  • Fine-tuning via Vertex AI tuning (Gemini) and Vertex AI Pipelines (open models, LoRA / QLoRA)
  • Every model version carries an evaluation card before it can be routed to
  • Shadow traffic: new versions receive mirrored requests and are scored offline before canary

Gateway responsibilities - Unified OpenAI-compatible and Vertex-native API for all agents - Per-agent token budgets and rate limits (Apigee), hard stops on runaway loops - Semantic cache in Memorystore keyed by embedding plus policy context - Prompt and response logging with DLP redaction before storage - Circuit breakers, retries with jitter, regional failover - Cost attribution labels: agent, use case, business unit Model supply chain - All self-hosted weights scanned, signed and stored in Artifact Registry / Model Registry - Fine-tuning via Vertex AI tuning (Gemini) and Vertex AI Pipelines (open models, LoRA / QLoRA) - Every model version carries an evaluation card before it can be routed to - Shadow traffic: new versions receive mirrored requests and are scored offline before canary

A latency SLO burn alert on a GKE service, resolved end to end within policy.

docs.title: Observability and telemetry
docs.html:
Observability and telemetry

Observing an agentic system means observing three things at once: the infrastructure it runs on, the behaviour of the agents, and the quality of their decisions. We instrument all three with OpenTelemetry using the GenAI semantic conventions, and land everything in one analytical store.

8.1 Telemetry pipeline

Figure 7. One trace ID follows a request through all layers; BigQuery is the join point for cost, quality and outcome.

8.2 Trace anatomy

Each agent episode is a root span with nested spans for every step. Attributes follow the OpenTelemetry gen_ai.* conventions plus our own agent.* namespace.

Span Key attributes
agent.episode agent.id, agent.version, trigger.type, incident.id, autonomy.level, outcome, total_cost_usd
agent.plan plan.steps, plan.hypotheses, plan.confidence
gen_ai.chat gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, router.tier, cache.hit, ttft_ms
retrieval.query index, top_k, latency_ms, docs_returned, acl_filtered
policy.decision rule.id, decision, risk.score, blast_radius
hitl.approval approver.id, wait_ms, decision
tool.call tool.name, mcp.server, idempotency_key, dry_run, status, side_effect.id
a2a.delegate from.agent, to.agent, task.id

8.3 Golden signals for agents

Operational

  • Episode success rate and latency (p50, p95)
  • Time to first token, tokens per second per model
  • Tool error rate and retry rate
  • Queue depth and age in Pub/Sub and Cloud Tasks
  • GPU / TPU utilisation, KV-cache utilisation

Quality

  • Plan precision (actions later judged correct)
  • Groundedness and faithfulness scores
  • Hallucinated tool or parameter rate
  • Human override and rollback rate
  • User feedback score from Chat and ITSM

Business

  • MTTD and MTTR by severity
  • Autonomous resolution rate
  • Toil hours removed per week
  • Change failure rate
  • Tickets deflected

Cost and safety

  • Cost per episode and per resolved incident
  • Cache hit rate and tier mix
  • Model Armor blocks, DLP findings
  • Policy denials and denied-then-retried attempts
  • Loop detection triggers and budget stops

8.4 Evaluation

Evaluation runs continuously, not just before release. Offline, every agent version runs against a golden set of replayed incidents in Vertex AI Pipelines and is scored by the Gen AI Evaluation Service (trajectory match, tool-use correctness, groundedness, safety) plus LLM-as-judge rubrics calibrated against human labels. Online, a sampled 5–10% of production episodes are scored asynchronously and every human override is turned into a new labelled test case. Quality metrics are exported to Cloud Monitoring so that a regression pages the owning team exactly like a latency regression.

8.5 SLOs

SLO Target Window
Agent platform availability 99.9% 28 days
Triage latency (event to classified) p95 < 5 s 28 days
P1 time to first diagnosis p90 < 3 min 28 days
Autonomous action correctness ≥ 99% rolling 500 actions
HITL request delivered to approver p99 < 30 s 28 days
Gateway error rate < 0.5% 7 days

docs.title: Scalability and resilience
docs.html:
Scalability and resilience

Inference scaling

  • GKE with GPU and TPU node pools; Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on queue depth and KV-cache utilisation, not CPU
  • GKE Inference Gateway for model-aware load balancing and LoRA adapter routing on shared base models
  • Custom compute classes with fallback between accelerator types; DWS flex-start for batch fine-tuning
  • SLMs on Cloud Run GPU scale to zero outside business hours
  • Gemini Provisioned Throughput sized to p70 load; pay-as-you-go absorbs burst

Orchestration scaling

  • Agent Engine scales agent runtimes horizontally; agents are stateless between steps with state in Sessions
  • Pub/Sub decouples ingestion from reasoning; ordering keys per incident preserve sequence
  • Cloud Tasks for rate-limited tool calls to fragile downstream systems
  • Workflows for long-running, durable plans that survive restarts
  • Priority lanes: P1 events bypass batch queues and reserve capacity

Failure handling

  • Idempotency keys on every mutating tool call; exactly-once side-effect ledger in Spanner
  • Circuit breakers per model and per tool; graceful degradation to L1 recommend-only mode
  • Loop guards: maximum steps, tokens and wall-clock per episode
  • Global kill switch per agent and per action type, propagated in < 10 s
  • Dead-letter topics with automated replay after fixes

Multi-region and DR

  • Active-active in two regions for gateway, orchestration and tools behind global load balancing
  • Spanner multi-region for side-effect ledger and graph; BigQuery multi-region for the lake
  • Vertex AI endpoints in both regions; in-house LLM warm standby
  • RPO ≈ 0 for approvals and actions, RTO < 15 min for the platform
  • If the agent platform is down, operations fall back to existing human runbooks: agents are never a single point of failure

Capacity model (illustrative)

Workload Volume per day Tier mix Peak concurrency
Event triage 2–5 million events ~98% SLM, 2% Flash 3,000 req/s
Incident diagnosis 5,000–20,000 episodes 60% in-house LLM, 40% Gemini 400 concurrent episodes
Service requests 30,000 requests 80% SLM, 20% Flash-Lite 150 req/s
Knowledge Q&A 50,000 queries 30% cache, 70% Flash 250 req/s

docs.title: Security and governance
docs.html:
Security and governance

Agents are a new class of privileged identity. The security model treats every agent as an untrusted-by-default workload that can be tricked, and places controls where a compromised prompt cannot reach them.

flowchart LR
subgraph P["VPC Service Controls perimeter: agentic-ops-prod"]
direction LR
A["Agent<br/>own service account"] --> G["Gateway<br/>Model Armor, DLP"]
G --> M["Models"]
A --> PD["Policy engine<br/>OPA rules as code"]
PD --> T["MCP tool<br/>executor SA, least privilege"]
T --> KMS["Cloud KMS CMEK"]
T --> SM["Secret Manager<br/>short-lived creds"]
end
T --> TGT["Target systems via PSC"]
A -. "audit" .-> AL["Cloud Audit Logs"] --> SO["Google SecOps"]
SCC["Security Command Center<br/>AI posture"] -.-> P

Figure 8. Reasoning identities and action identities are different service accounts. An agent can ask; only an executor can do.

Threat Control
Prompt injection via logs, tickets or documents Model Armor on inputs and retrieved content, content provenance tags, tools never accept instructions from data fields, policy engine independent of the LLM
Excessive agency Per-agent service accounts, IAM Conditions, action allow-lists per autonomy level, dry-run and blast-radius limits
Data exfiltration VPC-SC perimeters, Private Service Connect, egress deny by default, DLP on prompts and outputs, restricted data pinned to in-house models
Credential misuse No long-lived keys; Workload Identity and Secret Manager with short TTL; credentials held by executors only
Supply-chain compromise of models or tools Binary Authorization, signed model artefacts, MCP server allow-list, SBOMs, vulnerability scanning in Artifact Registry
Unaccountable decisions Immutable audit of prompt, context, plan, policy decision, approver and side effect; retained per regulatory schedule

Governance is run by an AI Ops Council (architecture, security, risk, operations) that owns the autonomy promotion process, the model approval list and the responsible-AI review for any new agent. Policies live as code in Git and deploy through the same pipeline as agents.

docs.html:
Full system architecture

This view places every platform component in its network trust zone and shows the physical and logical paths between them: public edge, hybrid transit (Interconnect and VPN), the hub network, the platform perimeter, the restricted enclave and the security management zone. Nothing in the platform core has a public IP; the only internet-facing surface is the global load balancer protected by Cloud Armor.

Figure 9. Full system view across trust zones. Solid lines are request paths; dotted lines are control, audit or backup paths.

Trust zones

Zone What lives there Entry rule Key controls
Z0 External Users, partners, SaaS, on-prem, other clouds Untrusted by default Device posture, identity federation, contractual controls for SaaS
Z1 Global edge Global ALB, Cloud Armor, IAP Only public IPs in the estate; HTTPS 443 only WAF (OWASP CRS), Adaptive Protection, bot management, rate limits, geo policy, TLS 1.2+ with modern cipher policy
Z2 Hybrid transit and hub Interconnect, HA VPN, NCC, Cloud Routers, NGFW, Secure Web Proxy, DNS BGP-learned routes from approved prefixes only MACsec on Interconnect, IPsec on VPN, IPS inspection on all north-south traffic, route filtering, FQDN egress allow-list
Z3 Platform core Apigee, agents, gateway, SLMs, tools, knowledge Through Apigee or NGFW only; VPC-SC perimeter on all Google APIs No external IPs (org policy), service mesh mTLS, per-agent service accounts, CMEK
Z4 Restricted enclave In-house LLM, regulated data, security telemetry with PII Perimeter bridge from LLM gateway only, one direction Separate VPC-SC perimeter, Confidential Computing, Cloud EKM or HSM keys, Access Approval, no internet egress at all
Z5 Security and management KMS, SCC, SecOps, log sinks, PAM Security team identities only, via PAM with justification Separate perimeter and folder, locked log buckets with retention, dual control on keys

docs.title: Network and connectivity
docs.html:
Network and connectivity

12.1 Hybrid connectivity: Interconnect primary, HA VPN backup

On-premises and other clouds connect through a hub-and-spoke design anchored on Network Connectivity Center. Dedicated Interconnect in the 99.99% topology (four circuits across two metros and two regions) carries production traffic with MACsec encryption at layer 2. HA VPN tunnels over the internet provide an encrypted backup path with lower BGP preference, and serve smaller sites and partners that cannot justify an Interconnect. Cross-Cloud Interconnect links to AWS and Azure where agents need to act on workloads there.

Figure 10. Hybrid transit. VPN tunnels advertise the same prefixes with a worse MED so they carry traffic only when Interconnect fails.

Link Purpose Encryption Availability Routing
Dedicated Interconnect (4 × 10/100G) Primary data centre connectivity, telemetry ingest, agent actions on-prem MACsec; optional HA VPN over Interconnect for IPsec end to end on regulated flows 99.99% SLA topology BGP, MED 100, custom advertised ranges only
HA VPN (2 gateways × 2 tunnels) Backup path, branch sites, partners IKEv2 IPsec, AES-256-GCM 99.99% SLA per gateway pair BGP, MED 200 for DC prefixes
Partner HA VPN Managed-service vendors needing access to a scoped partner spoke IKEv2 IPsec with certificate authentication 99.99% Only the partner spoke's /24 advertised; NGFW rules by secure tag
Cross-Cloud Interconnect Agent actions and telemetry for AWS and Azure workloads MACsec 99.99% with redundant pairs BGP to NCC hub
Private Service Connect Google APIs, Apigee southbound, MCP tools into workload projects TLS inside Google network Regional Consumer endpoints, no VPC peering

12.2 VPC and IP design

A dedicated network hub project hosts the NCC hub, Cloud Routers, NGFW endpoints, Secure Web Proxy and DNS. Platform, nonprod and restricted workloads each get their own Shared VPC host project so that firewall and perimeter changes can be scoped. The ranges below are illustrative and sized for GKE with alias IPs.

Network Range Subnets
Hub transit 10.0.0.0/20 Cloud Router interfaces, NGFW endpoints, SWP, PSC endpoints for Google APIs (10.0.8.0/24)
Prod platform (region A) 10.16.0.0/16 Nodes 10.16.0.0/20; pods 10.16.64.0/18; services 10.16.128.0/20; Cloud Run direct VPC egress 10.16.16.0/20; PSC consumer 10.16.200.0/24; proxy-only 10.16.250.0/23
Prod platform (region B) 10.17.0.0/16 Mirror of region A
Restricted enclave 10.32.0.0/16 Confidential GKE nodes 10.32.0.0/20; pods 10.32.64.0/18; no Cloud NAT, no internet routes
Nonprod 10.48.0.0/15 Dev, test, eval replay
Partner spoke 10.60.0.0/24 Vendor jump services behind IAP only
On-prem (advertised to GCP) 172.16.0.0/12 Summarised per data centre

12.3 Private access to Google and platform services

  • Google APIs. A PSC endpoint for the vpc-sc API bundle, with private Cloud DNS zones mapping *.googleapis.com to it. Vertex AI, BigQuery, Storage and all other API calls stay on Google's network and are forced through VPC-SC checks.
  • On-prem to Google APIs. On-prem DNS forwards googleapis.com to Cloud DNS inbound forwarders; Cloud Routers advertise the PSC endpoint range over Interconnect, so on-prem collectors can write telemetry without internet paths.
  • Apigee X. Northbound through the global ALB; southbound to agents through PSC, with no VPC peering between Apigee's tenant network and ours.
  • MCP tool reach. Tools that must act inside a business unit's VPC are published as PSC service attachments from that VPC, so the platform gets one IP per tool with no broad network routes to workload subnets.
  • DNS security. Private zones per environment, DNSSEC on public zones, and DNS response policies that block resolution of unapproved external domains from the platform core.

12.4 Ingress paths

Caller Path Authentication
Employees (ops console, Gemini Enterprise) Chrome Enterprise Premium, Cloud Armor, global ALB, IAP, Apigee Workforce SSO with phishing-resistant MFA, device posture, context-aware access levels
Google Chat approvals Google Chat app to Cloud Run endpoint behind ALB Google-signed bearer token verified on every event
Slack and Teams bots Cloud Armor (allow-listed source ranges), ALB, Apigee Request signature verification plus mTLS where supported
ITSM and alerting webhooks Cloud Armor, ALB, Apigee, Pub/Sub OAuth client credentials or HMAC signatures, replay protection
On-prem monitoring and logs Interconnect, NGFW, internal ALB or Pub/Sub via PSC Workload Identity Federation with short-lived tokens
Partner engineers HA VPN to partner spoke, then IAP TCP forwarding Federated partner identity, PAM time-bound grant

12.5 Egress control

Egress is denied by default at the hierarchical firewall policy. Model-serving nodes and the restricted enclave have no egress at all. Agents and MCP tools that must call SaaS go through Secure Web Proxy with an FQDN allow-list per tool service account (for example only the ServiceNow instance for the ITSM executor), TLS inspection where policy allows, and Cloud NAT with static IPs that SaaS vendors can allow-list. Model weights and container images are never pulled at runtime; they enter only through the build project, are scanned and signed, and are served from Artifact Registry.

12.6 East-west and microsegmentation

Inside the perimeter, Cloud Service Mesh enforces mTLS with workload identities for every hop, and authorization policies state which agent may call which tool service (for example the incident agent may call the Kubernetes executor but not the IAM executor). Cloud NGFW network firewall policies use IAM-governed secure tags rather than IP ranges, so a compromised workload cannot relabel itself into a broader rule.

12.7 Administrative access

There are no bastion hosts with public IPs and no standing admin roles. Engineers reach the console and APIs through Chrome Enterprise Premium with context-aware access, reach VMs and nodes through IAP TCP forwarding, and gain elevated roles only through Privileged Access Manager with a justification, an approver and an expiry. Two break-glass accounts protected by hardware security keys exist per perimeter; any use pages the security on-call and opens a SecOps case automatically.

docs.title: Security gates
docs.html:
Security gates

Security is enforced as a chain of gates that every request and every release must pass. Each gate is deterministic, independently owned, logged, and fails closed. No single gate relies on the LLM behaving correctly.

13.1 Runtime gate chain

Figure 11. Runtime gates in request order. Each gate emits a policy.decision span and an audit log entry.

Gate Checks Services Owner On failure
G1 Edge Volumetric and L7 DDoS, OWASP rules, bot scores, geo, per-client rate limits Cloud Armor Enterprise, Adaptive Protection, global ALB Network security 403 or throttle; signature to SecOps
G2 Identity and context User SSO + MFA, device posture, access level; workload federation for machines IAP, Chrome Enterprise Premium, Cloud Identity, Workload Identity Federation Identity team Deny; risky sign-in alert
G3 API contract OAuth scopes, JWT validation, JSON schema, payload size, spike arrest, token quotas Apigee X API platform 4xx with reason code
G4 Input safety Prompt injection and jailbreak detection, malicious URLs, PII and secrets detection and redaction Model Armor, Sensitive Data Protection AI security Block or redact; quarantine sample
G5 Agent authorisation Is this caller allowed to invoke this agent; is this agent allowed to delegate to that agent over A2A; mesh authz IAM, Agent Engine identity, Cloud Service Mesh Platform team Deny delegation
G6 Model gateway Data classification pins restricted content to in-house models; per-agent budget; loop guard LLM gateway, Apigee quotas Platform team Reroute or stop episode
G7 Retrieval ACL Only documents and records the on-behalf-of user may read; provenance tag on each chunk Vertex AI Search ACLs, RAG metadata filters, Spanner row policies Data governance Filter silently; log counts
G8 Output safety Response screening, sensitive data leak check, groundedness threshold, tool-call schema validation Model Armor, DLP, Gen AI evaluation checks in-line AI security Block, regenerate, or downgrade to recommend-only
G9 Action policy Action allow-list per autonomy level, blast radius, change freeze windows, target criticality, rate of change OPA on Cloud Run, policy bundles from Git Service owners + AI Ops Council Deny or require G10
G10 Human approval Named approver in owning group, evidence reviewed, separation of duties (requester cannot approve) HITL service, Workflows, Google Chat cards Service owners Reject, escalate, or time out
G11 Execution guard Just-in-time scoped credentials, dry-run, idempotency, network reachability through NGFW, rate limits on target Executor SAs, Secret Manager, PAM, Cloud NGFW, Cloud Tasks Platform team Abort, rollback, demote action type
G12 Verify and audit Post-conditions met, side-effect ledger written, immutable audit record, anomaly detection Spanner ledger, Cloud Audit Logs, SecOps detections Security operations Auto-rollback and incident

13.2 Gates under attack: indirect prompt injection

The most likely attack on an ops agent is an instruction hidden in data it reads, such as a crafted log line or ticket comment. The flow below shows how several independent gates stop it even if the model is fooled.

sequenceDiagram
autonumber
participant ATK as Attacker
participant APP as Workload logs
participant INC as Incident agent
participant MA as Model Armor
participant GW as LLM gateway
participant PDP as Policy engine
participant IAMT as IAM executor
participant SOC as Google SecOps
ATK->>APP: writes log line with hidden instruction to grant owner role
INC->>APP: retrieves logs during diagnosis
INC->>MA: screen retrieved content (G4)
MA-->>INC: injection detected, span flagged, content quarantined
INC->>GW: reason with quarantined content removed
GW-->>INC: plan without IAM step
Note over INC,PDP: Suppose screening had missed it and the model proposed the grant
INC->>PDP: authorise "grant roles/owner" (G9)
PDP-->>INC: deny, action not in incident agent allow-list
INC-xIAMT: no call possible, incident agent SA lacks invoker role (G5)
PDP-)SOC: deny event with trace_id
MA-)SOC: injection finding with source log
SOC->>SOC: correlate, open case, SOAR tags source workload

Figure 12. Defence in depth: content screening, policy allow-lists and IAM each stop the attack on their own.

13.3 Delivery gates

Every agent, prompt, tool, policy bundle and model version reaches production only through the pipeline below. Binary Authorization on GKE and Cloud Run rejects any image without the full set of attestations.

flowchart LR
C["Commit<br/>signed, reviewed"] --> D1{"D1 Code scan<br/>SAST, secrets, IaC lint"}
D1 --> D2{"D2 Dependencies<br/>SCA, licence, SBOM"}
D2 --> D3{"D3 Image and model<br/>vuln scan, weight hash, signature"}
D3 --> D4{"D4 Policy tests<br/>OPA unit tests, tool contracts"}
D4 --> D5{"D5 Offline eval<br/>quality and safety scores"}
D5 --> D6{"D6 Red team<br/>injection and misuse suites"}
D6 --> D7{"D7 Attest and approve<br/>Binary Authorization, change record"}
D7 --> D8{"D8 Progressive rollout<br/>shadow, canary, SLO guard"}
D8 --> PRD["Production"]
D1 -- "fail" --> STOP["Block release"]
D3 -- "fail" --> STOP
D5 -- "regression" --> STOP
D6 -- "fail" --> STOP
D8 -- "SLO breach" --> RBK["Automatic rollback"]

Figure 13. Delivery gates, implemented with Cloud Build, Artifact Analysis, Vertex AI Pipelines, Binary Authorization and Cloud Deploy.

13.4 Encryption and key management

Where Mechanism Keys
Internet to edge TLS 1.2+ (1.3 preferred), HSTS, SSL policy restricting ciphers Certificate Manager managed certificates
Hybrid links MACsec on Interconnect; IPsec on HA VPN; optional HA VPN over Interconnect MACsec CAK keys rotated quarterly; IKE certificates from Certificate Authority Service
Service to service mTLS through Cloud Service Mesh Mesh CA, 24-hour workload certificates
Data at rest, platform CMEK on BigQuery, Spanner, AlloyDB, GCS, Vertex AI resources, Pub/Sub, Artifact Registry Cloud KMS with Cloud HSM, per-perimeter key rings, automatic rotation
Restricted enclave CMEK with externally held keys; Confidential GKE nodes (confidential GPUs where supported) for data in use Cloud EKM with Key Access Justifications
Provider access Access Transparency logs and Access Approval for Google personnel access Approval by security leads

13.5 Detection and response for the agent platform

  • Network telemetry. VPC Flow Logs on all subnets, Cloud NGFW IPS threat logs, Packet Mirroring into Cloud IDS for the restricted enclave, Interconnect and VPN tunnel metrics in Cloud Monitoring.
  • Posture. Security Command Center Enterprise with AI protection for model, agent and dataset inventory, misconfiguration findings, and toxic-combination analysis.
  • Agent-specific detections in Google SecOps. An agent calling a tool it has never used, a spike in policy denials, privileged actions outside change windows, token spend far above baseline, repeated Model Armor findings from one data source, or an executor credential used from an unexpected network.
  • Automated containment. SOAR playbooks can flip an agent's kill switch, disable its service account, revoke PAM grants, isolate a workload with a deny tag, or pin the router to recommend-only mode, all in under a minute.
  • Evidence. Audit and agent-lake logs are written to locked log buckets with retention policies, giving tamper-evident records for investigations and regulators.

docs.title: FinOps for intelligence
docs.html:
FinOps for intelligence

  • Attribute everything. Labels on every model call (agent, use case, cost centre) flow into BigQuery billing export joined with the agent lake, giving cost per resolved incident and per business outcome.
  • Push work down the tiers. Target 70%+ of tokens on SLMs and cache; review the tier mix monthly and distil frequent Gemini tasks into SLMs.
  • Buy baseline, rent burst. Provisioned Throughput and committed-use discounts for GPUs/TPUs cover steady load; spot and DWS flex-start for training and batch evaluation.
  • Budgets as guardrails. Per-agent daily token budgets enforced at the gateway, with Cloud Billing budgets and Pub/Sub alerts on anomalies.
  • Context discipline. Context caching for large stable prompts, retrieval over stuffing, and summarised memory rather than raw history.

Risks and key decisions

Decision or risk Position Mitigation or rationale
Agent runtime: Agent Engine vs self-hosted on GKE Agent Engine by default; GKE for agents needing custom networking or extreme throughput ADK runs on both, so the choice is reversible per agent
Build in-house LLMs Fine-tune open weights, do not pre-train Restricted data and cost at scale justify it; pre-training does not
Vendor concentration on Google Cloud Accept, with open protocols at the seams MCP, A2A, OTel, OCI and Terraform keep migration feasible
Over-automation causing outages Autonomy earned per action type Shadow mode, blast-radius limits, kill switch, automatic demotion

docs.title: Intent and principles
docs.html:
Intent and principles

Agentic Ops replaces ticket-driven, human-routed operations with a mesh of specialised agents that observe signals, reason over enterprise context, plan, act through governed tools, and learn from outcomes. The principles are cloud-neutral and identical to the Google Cloud edition; only the services change.

Agents are workloads

Every agent has an IAM identity, a versioned spec, an SLO, a budget, an owner and a kill switch, and runs in AgentCore Runtime like any production service.

Right model for the job

SLMs on Inferentia for volume, in-house LLMs on EKS for restricted data, Bedrock models (Amazon Nova, Anthropic Claude and others) for deep reasoning. One gateway decides.

Autonomy is earned

Each action type starts in shadow mode and graduates through autonomy levels based on measured precision, blast radius and reversibility.

Everything is a trace

AgentCore Observability and ADOT emit OpenTelemetry spans for every step, joined by one trace ID from alarm to outcome in X-Ray and CloudWatch.

Policy outside the prompt

AgentCore Policy (Cedar) intercepts every tool call, and SCPs and IAM boundaries cap what any agent role can ever do, regardless of what the model says.

Open protocols

MCP through AgentCore Gateway, A2A between agents, OpenTelemetry, OCI images and Terraform or CDK keep every seam portable.

docs.title: End-to-end flow
docs.html:
End-to-end flow

A CloudWatch alarm, ticket, chat message or EventBridge event enters through the edge, passes Bedrock Guardrails, is triaged by an SLM and handed to the supervisor on AgentCore Runtime. The supervisor delegates over A2A, domain agents ground themselves in Knowledge Bases, Neptune topology and AgentCore Memory, and every proposed action is checked by AgentCore Policy before an MCP tool behind AgentCore Gateway touches production.

Figure 1. Signal-to-outcome flow on AWS. Dotted lines are asynchronous telemetry and learning paths.

The operating loop

Stage What happens Primary services Emitted telemetry
1. Perceive Normalise the trigger into a canonical event, dedupe, correlate with open incidents. EventBridge, SQS FIFO, Kinesis agent.event.received, correlation ratio
2. Ground Retrieve topology, recent changes (CloudTrail, Config), runbooks, similar incidents, live metrics. Neptune Analytics, Knowledge Bases, AgentCore Memory, CloudWatch retrieval latency, hit rate
3. Reason and plan Rank hypotheses, produce a typed plan with expected effects and rollback. LLM gateway, Bedrock, in-house LLM tokens, model, TTFT
4. Authorise Cedar policies evaluate each tool call; risky steps route to a human. AgentCore Policy, Step Functions, Slack / Teams decision, policy ID, approval latency
5. Act Execute via MCP tools and SSM Automation with idempotency and dry-run. AgentCore Gateway, Systems Manager, Lambda tool status, side-effect ID
6. Learn Close ticket, write episodic memory, score with evaluations, feed tuning sets. AgentCore Memory, AgentCore Evaluations, S3 Tables outcome, MTTR, feedback

docs.title: Agent topology
docs.html:
Agent topology

A hierarchical mesh: supervisor, specialists and narrow executors. Agents are built with the Strands Agents SDK (any framework works on AgentCore Runtime), registered in AgentCore Registry, and authenticated to each other and to tools through AgentCore Identity.

flowchart TB
U["Operators, SREs, business users"] --> GE["Quick Suite, Slack, Teams front door"]
GE --> SUP["Ops Supervisor<br/>Bedrock frontier model"]
EVT["EventBridge stream"] --> TRI["Triage agent<br/>SLM"]
TRI --> SUP
REG[("AgentCore Registry<br/>A2A agent cards")] -.-> SUP
SUP --> INC["Incident and RCA agent"]
SUP --> CHG["Change and release agent"]
SUP --> CAP["Capacity and FinOps agent"]
SUP --> SEC["SecOps agent"]
SUP --> KNW["Knowledge agent"]
SUP --> SVC["Service request agent"]
INC --> EX1["EKS executor"]
INC --> EX2["SSM Automation executor"]
CHG --> EX3["IaC executor<br/>CloudFormation, Terraform"]
CHG --> EX4["CI/CD executor<br/>CodePipeline"]
CAP --> EX5["Cost and quota executor"]
SEC --> EX6["Containment executor<br/>Security Hub, GuardDuty"]
SVC --> EX7["ITSM executor"]
KNW --> EX8["Runbook writer"]

Figure 2. Executors hold the only IAM roles that can mutate systems.

Agent Responsibility Default model tier Key tools Starting autonomy
Triage Classify, dedupe, prioritise every signal SLM on Inferentia EventBridge, CMDB lookup L4
Ops Supervisor Decompose goals, delegate, arbitrate Bedrock frontier model A2A, Registry L3
Incident and RCA Correlate, diagnose, remediate In-house LLM, Bedrock for multimodal CloudWatch, X-Ray, SSM, EKS MCP L1 then L3
Change and release Risk-score changes, canaries, rollback Bedrock mid-tier model CodePipeline, CloudFormation, AppConfig L2
Capacity and FinOps Rightsizing, Savings Plans, spend anomalies SLM + Cost Explorer data Compute Optimizer, Cost Anomaly Detection L2
SecOps Finding triage, enrichment, containment In-house LLM for restricted data Security Hub, GuardDuty, Detective L1
Knowledge Answer questions, keep runbooks current Bedrock fast model Knowledge Bases, Kendra L3
Service request Fulfil standard requests SLM + fast model ServiceNow, IAM Identity Center, Service Catalog L3

Autonomy levels

Level Behaviour
L0 Observe Shadow mode; AgentCore Policy in log-only mode.
L1 Recommend Plan presented; a human executes.
L2 Approve Executes after a named approver responds to a Step Functions task token.
L3 Notify Executes, then notifies, with a rollback window.
L4 Autonomous Executes and closes; reviewed by sampling and evaluations.

Promotion rule. One level up after 200 executions or 30 days at ≥ 98% plan precision, zero severity-1 side effects, a tested rollback and service-owner sign-off. Any agent-caused severity-1 demotes that action type two levels automatically.

docs.html:
Model strategy and routing

Tier Models Hosting Used for
SLM Fine-tuned 1–9B open models, distilled classifiers, Bedrock distilled models EKS with Karpenter on Inferentia2 or G-family GPUs; SageMaker endpoints for steady load Triage, intent, extraction, log parsing, PII tagging, routing
In-house LLM Fine-tuned open-weight 30–70B models EKS on Trainium / P5 with vLLM or Neuron; optionally Bedrock Custom Model Import for serverless hosting inside our account boundary Reasoning over restricted data, RCA narratives, security telemetry
Frontier Amazon Nova family, Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, Mistral on Bedrock (latest GA versions) Bedrock on-demand with cross-Region inference profiles; Provisioned Throughput for baseline Complex planning, long context, multimodal, code generation 
flowchart TD
IN["Request from agent<br/>capability, data class, budget, SLO"] --> C1{"Semantic cache hit<br/>ElastiCache Valkey"}
C1 -- "yes" --> OUT["Return cached"]
C1 -- "no" --> C2{"Restricted or regulated data?"}
C2 -- "yes" --> LLM["In-house LLM<br/>enclave account"]
C2 -- "no" --> C3{"Complexity score"}
C3 -- "low" --> SLM["SLM tier"]
C3 -- "medium" --> MID["Bedrock fast model"]
C3 -- "high or multimodal" --> TOP["Bedrock frontier model"]
SLM --> V{"Confidence above threshold?"}
V -- "no" --> MID
V -- "yes" --> OUT2["Return and cache"]
MID --> OUT2
TOP --> OUT2
LLM --> OUT2
TOP -. "throttle or 5xx" .-> FB["Cross-Region inference profile,<br/>then alternate model family"]

Figure 3. Cascade routing. Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing can serve as the within-family router; our gateway owns cross-tier decisions.

The gateway also applies Bedrock prompt caching for large stable system prompts, enforces per-agent token budgets, tags every call with cost-allocation tags, and invokes Bedrock Guardrails on both input and output.

docs.title: Observability and telemetry
docs.html:
Observability and telemetry

AgentCore Observability emits OpenTelemetry-compatible traces for agent sessions, model calls and tool invocations into CloudWatch, with a GenAI observability view. ADOT collectors on EKS and Lambda extensions cover the rest, and everything lands in an analytical lake for cost, quality and outcome analysis.

Figure 7. Telemetry pipeline on AWS. Quality metrics from evaluations are published back into CloudWatch so they can page owners like latency does.

Trace anatomy

Span Key attributes
agent.episode agent.id, agent.version, session.id, trigger.type, incident.id, autonomy.level, outcome, cost_usd
gen_ai.chat gen_ai.request.model (Bedrock model ID or inference profile), input/output tokens, router.tier, cache.hit, guardrail.action
retrieval.query knowledge_base.id, top_k, latency_ms, acl_filtered
policy.decision cedar.policy_id, decision, mode (enforce or log-only), risk.score
hitl.approval approver.id, task_token_wait_ms, decision
tool.call gateway.target, ssm.execution_id, idempotency_key, dry_run, status

Operational

  • Episode success and latency
  • TTFT and tokens per second per model
  • Bedrock throttles and cross-Region spillover
  • SQS age and depth
  • Neuron core and GPU utilisation

Quality

  • Plan precision
  • Groundedness and correctness (AgentCore Evaluations)
  • Hallucinated tool or parameter rate
  • Human override and rollback rate

Business

  • MTTD and MTTR
  • Autonomous resolution rate
  • Toil hours removed
  • Change failure rate

Cost and safety

  • Cost per episode and per resolved incident
  • Guardrail interventions
  • Policy denials
  • Loop and budget stops

SLOs

SLO Target
Agent platform availability 99.9% over 28 days
Triage latency p95 < 5 s
P1 time to first diagnosis p90 < 3 min
Autonomous action correctness ≥ 99% over rolling 500 actions
Approval card delivered p99 < 30 s

docs.title: Scalability and resilience
docs.html:
Scalability and resilience

Inference scaling

  • EKS with Karpenter node pools across Inferentia, Trainium and GPU instance families
  • KEDA scaling on queue depth and KV-cache utilisation
  • Bedrock cross-Region inference profiles absorb burst
  • Provisioned Throughput sized to steady baseline
  • Capacity Blocks or Savings Plans for reserved accelerators

Orchestration scaling

  • AgentCore Runtime isolates each session in its own microVM and scales automatically
  • EventBridge and SQS decouple ingest from reasoning; FIFO groups per incident
  • Step Functions for long-running durable plans
  • Priority queues reserve capacity for P1

Failure handling

  • Idempotency keys and a DynamoDB side-effect ledger
  • Circuit breakers per model and tool; degrade to recommend-only
  • Step, token and time caps per episode
  • Kill switch via AppConfig feature flags, < 10 s propagation
  • DLQs with replay

Multi-Region and DR

  • Active-active in two Regions behind Route 53 health-checked routing
  • DynamoDB global tables for ledger and approvals
  • Aurora Global Database and Neptune replicas

docs.title: Network and connectivity
docs.html:
Network and connectivity

12.1 Direct Connect primary, Site-to-Site VPN backup

Data centres connect through Dedicated Direct Connect in the maximum-resiliency model: four connections across two Direct Connect locations per Region pair, with MACsec on 10 and 100 Gbps ports. Transit virtual interfaces land on a Direct Connect gateway associated with Transit Gateways in each Region. Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN attachments on the Transit Gateways carry the same prefixes with a longer AS path, so they only take traffic when Direct Connect fails; they also serve branches and partners. Cloud WAN can replace per-Region Transit Gateways for global segmentation as the estate grows.

Figure 10. Hybrid transit on AWS. VPN paths are dashed amber; the enclave is reachable only through PrivateLink.

Link Purpose Encryption Routing
Dedicated Direct Connect (4 × 10/100G) Primary DC connectivity, telemetry, on-prem actions MACsec; optional private IP VPN over DX for IPsec end to end Transit VIF to DX gateway, BGP communities for local preference
Site-to-Site VPN (accelerated) Backup path, branches, partners IKEv2 IPsec, AES-256-GCM BGP, AS-path prepended
Partner VPN Vendors into a scoped partner VPC IPsec, certificate auth via Private CA Isolated TGW route table
Partner interconnect to other clouds Actions on Azure and Google Cloud workloads MACsec or IPsec BGP to TGW / Cloud WAN
PrivateLink and VPC Lattice AWS services, tools in workload accounts, enclave access TLS No routing between VPCs needed

12.2 VPC and IP design

IP addressing is allocated by VPC IPAM from the network account. Platform VPCs are shared to platform accounts with AWS RAM; inspection is centralised in an inspection VPC with Network Firewall in appliance mode on the Transit Gateway.

Network Range Notes
Inspection VPC 10.0.0.0/22 Network Firewall endpoints per AZ, TGW attachment subnets
Egress VPC 10.0.4.0/22 NAT gateways behind Network Firewall domain allow-list
Platform prod (Region A) 10.16.0.0/16 Private subnets per AZ for EKS (prefix delegation), AgentCore VPC config, endpoints
Platform prod (Region B) 10.17.0.0/16 Mirror
Restricted enclave 10.32.0.0/16 No IGW, no NAT, no TGW route to the internet
Nonprod 10.48.0.0/15 Separate TGW route table
On-prem 172.16.0.0/12 Summarised per data centre

12.3 Private access, egress and east-west

  • AWS services. Interface endpoints for Bedrock runtime, AgentCore, STS, KMS, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch, SSM and others, plus gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB, all with endpoint policies restricted to our organisation.
  • DNS. Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints for hybrid resolution, private hosted zones shared through RAM, and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall blocking unapproved domains.
  • Egress. Denied by default. SaaS calls from executors leave through the egress VPC, where Network Firewall stateful rules allow only listed SNI domains per source CIDR, and NAT gateways present fixed IPs that SaaS vendors can allow-list. Model and enclave subnets have no egress path.
  • East-west. VPC Lattice service networks with IAM auth policies define which agent may call which tool; security groups reference each other rather than CIDRs.
  • Admin access. No bastions: Systems Manager Session Manager for instances and nodes, Verified Access for internal web tools, temporary elevated access through an approval workflow on IAM Identity Center permission sets, and break-glass IAM users with hardware MFA monitored by GuardDuty and EventBridge.

Security gates

13.1 Runtime gate chain

Figure 11. Runtime gates on AWS. Each gate emits a policy.decision span and a CloudTrail or application audit event.

Gate Checks Services On failure
G1 Edge DDoS, managed rule groups, bot control, geo, rate limits CloudFront, WAF, Shield Advanced Block or challenge
G2 Identity SSO + MFA, device posture, workload identity IAM Identity Center, Cognito, Verified Access, IAM Roles Anywhere Deny
G3 API contract JWT authoriser, request validation, throttling, payload limits API Gateway, Lambda authorisers 4xx with reason
G4 Input safety Prompt attacks, denied topics, PII and secrets Bedrock Guardrails, Comprehend PII Block or mask
G5 Agent authorisation Inbound and outbound agent identity, A2A delegation rights AgentCore Identity, IAM, VPC Lattice auth Deny delegation
G6 Model gateway Data class pins restricted content to the enclave; budgets; loop guard LLM gateway, usage plans Reroute or stop
G7 Retrieval ACL Only entitled documents, provenance tagged Knowledge Base metadata filters, Lake Formation Filter
G8 Output safety Response filters, contextual grounding check, tool schema validation Bedrock Guardrails (contextual grounding), Automated Reasoning checks Block or downgrade
G9 Action policy Tool allow-lists, parameters, blast radius, change windows AgentCore Policy (Cedar) in Gateway path Deny or require G10
G10 Human approval Named approver, separation of duties Step Functions task tokens, SSM Change Manager Reject or escalate
G11 Execution guard Short-lived STS credentials, session policies, dry-run, network path via Network Firewall STS, SSM Automation, Lambda Abort and rollback
G12 Verify and audit Post-conditions, ledger, immutable audit, anomaly detection DynamoDB ledger, CloudTrail Lake, GuardDuty, Security Lake Rollback and incident

participant ATK as Attacker

AGW-->>INC: denied

D1 --> D2{"D2 Dependencies<br/>Inspector SBOM, licence"}

D8 -- "alarm" --> RBK["Automatic rollback"]

Figure 13. Delivery gates in CodePipeline, with IAM Access Analyzer policy checks and signature verification at EKS admission.

13.4 Encryption and key management

Where Mechanism Keys
Internet to edge TLS 1.2+ with CloudFront security policy ACM certificates
Hybrid links MACsec on Direct Connect; IPsec on VPN MACsec CKN/CAK in Secrets Manager; VPN certs from Private CA
Service to service TLS everywhere; mTLS on API Gateway custom domains and VPC Lattice where required Private CA
At rest, platform KMS CMKs on S3, DynamoDB, Aurora, OpenSearch, Bedrock resources, AgentCore Memory, EBS, ECR Per-account keys, automatic rotation, key policies scoped to roles
Restricted enclave KMS external key store (XKS) or CloudHSM-backed custom key store Keys held outside AWS or in dedicated HSMs

13.5 Detection and response

  • Signals. VPC Flow Logs, Network Firewall alerts, Route 53 Resolver query logs, CloudTrail data events, GuardDuty (including EKS runtime and Lambda protection), Inspector and Macie findings, all normalised to OCSF in Security Lake.
  • Agent-specific detections. New tool usage by an agent, spikes in Cedar denials or Guardrails interventions, privileged API calls outside change windows, token spend far above baseline, or an executor role used from an unexpected VPC endpoint.
  • Automated containment. EventBridge rules trigger Step Functions or SOAR playbooks that flip the AppConfig kill switch, attach a deny-all session policy, revoke Identity Center sessions, or isolate a workload's security group.

docs.title: FinOps for intelligence
docs.html:
FinOps for intelligence

  • Attribute everything. Cost-allocation tags and Bedrock application inference profiles per agent and use case, joined with the agent lake in Athena for cost per resolved incident.
  • Push work down the tiers. Target 70%+ of tokens on SLMs and cache; use Bedrock Model Distillation to move frequent frontier tasks into smaller models.
  • Buy baseline, rent burst. Provisioned Throughput and Savings Plans for steady load; Spot and Capacity Blocks for training and batch evaluation; Bedrock batch inference at lower cost for offline scoring.
  • Budgets as guardrails. AWS Budgets actions and Cost Anomaly Detection alerts, plus hard per-agent token caps at the gateway.
  • Context discipline. Prompt caching, retrieval over stuffing, summarised memory.

docs.title: 0001. Put one gateway in front of every model
docs.html:
0001. Put one gateway in front of every model

  • Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-16

Context

Agents will use SLMs, in-house LLMs and several frontier models. If each team calls models directly, we lose cost attribution, cannot enforce which data reaches which model, cannot fail over, and cannot change models without rewriting agents.

Decision

All model traffic goes through a single LLM gateway (layer L3). Agents request a capability and a data class; the gateway chooses the model, applies the semantic cache, enforces per-agent token budgets, pins restricted data to the in-house tier, records cost labels and handles regional failover.

Consequences

  • Model swaps become a routing change, not an agent release.
  • Cost per agent, use case and incident becomes measurable.
  • The gateway is now critical infrastructure: it needs multi-region deployment, its own SLO and circuit breakers.
  • Some managed features (for example vendor prompt routing) are used behind the gateway rather than instead of it.

Alternatives considered

Option Why not
Direct SDK calls from agents No central control of data class, budget or failover.
Vendor-only router Cannot route to in-house models or across clouds.

docs.title: 0002. Set autonomy per action type, earned with evidence
docs.html:
0002. Set autonomy per action type, earned with evidence

  • Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-16

Context

Granting autonomy per agent forces an all-or-nothing choice: either the incident agent can do everything it knows how to do, or nothing. Risk teams cannot approve that, and operators lose the easy wins.

Decision

Autonomy is configured per action type on a five-level scale (L0 Observe to L4 Autonomous). Promotion is one level at a time against an evidence gate (≥ 200 executions or 30 days, ≥ 98% plan precision, zero agent-caused Sev-1, exercised rollback, owner sign-off). Any agent-caused Sev-1 demotes the action type two levels automatically. See Earned autonomy.

Consequences

  • Low-risk, reversible actions automate quickly; high-risk ones stay gated.
  • Requires plan-precision measurement, which in turn requires evaluation and labelling.
  • Policy configuration grows with the number of action types; it must live in Git with tests.

Alternatives considered

Option Why not
Autonomy per agent Too coarse; blocks safe automation or allows unsafe.
Fixed human approval for everything Removes most of the value; approval fatigue.

docs.title: 0003. Enforce action policy in a deterministic service, not the prompt
docs.html:
0003. Enforce action policy in a deterministic service, not the prompt

  • Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-16

Context

Agents read untrusted content: logs, tickets, documents, web pages. Indirect prompt injection (OWASP LLM01) can make a model propose actions its instructions forbid. Instructions in a system prompt are not a security control.

Decision

Every tool call passes a deterministic policy decision point before execution: OPA on Google Cloud, AgentCore Policy (Cedar) on AWS. Policies are code in Git, unit-tested in the delivery pipeline (gate D4), and evaluated outside the model's process. The model's output is treated as a request, never as an authorisation.

Consequences

  • A fooled model can propose a harmful action but cannot execute it.
  • Every decision is logged with the rule that made it, which simplifies audit.
  • Policy latency is on the hot path; keep it in-region and cache bundles.

Alternatives considered

Option Why not
System-prompt rules only Bypassable by injection; not auditable.
LLM-as-judge for authorisation Non-deterministic and itself injectable.

docs.title: 0004. Separate reasoning identities from action identities
docs.html:
0004. Separate reasoning identities from action identities

  • Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-16

Context

If the identity an agent reasons under can also change production, any compromise of the reasoning path (prompt injection, a bad model version, a bug) is a compromise of production.

Decision

Agents run under a reasoning identity that can call models, retrieval and other agents but holds no permission to mutate systems. Narrow executor services, one per tool family, hold the only mutating credentials, issued just in time and scoped per call. Agents may invoke only the executors listed in their spec.

Consequences

  • Blast radius of a compromised agent is limited to what its permitted executors can do, after policy.
  • More identities to manage; automate creation from the agent spec.
  • Executors become a reusable, audited catalogue shared across agents.

Alternatives considered

Option Why not
One service account per agent with all permissions Policy becomes the only control; no defence in depth.

docs.title: 0005. Fine-tune open-weight models; do not pre-train
docs.html:
0005. Fine-tune open-weight models; do not pre-train

  • Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-16

Context

Some data (security telemetry, regulated customer data) must stay inside our perimeter, and high-volume tasks are cheaper on small models. Pre-training a model from scratch is expensive and slow, and rarely beats a well-tuned open-weight base on narrow operational tasks.

Decision

Build in-house capability by fine-tuning open-weight models: 1–9B parameter SLMs for triage and extraction, 30–70B models for reasoning over restricted data. Host them in the restricted enclave with signed weights, evaluation cards and shadow traffic before release. Distil frequent frontier-model tasks into SLMs over time.

Consequences

  • Restricted data never leaves the perimeter; cost per token falls at high utilisation.
  • We own model lifecycle: tuning pipelines, evaluation, accelerator capacity.
  • Licence terms of each open-weight base must be reviewed.

Alternatives considered

Option Why not
Pre-train our own model Cost and time not justified for operations tasks.
Frontier API for everything Cannot meet data residency for restricted data; higher cost at volume.

docs.title: 0006. Use the cloud's managed agent runtime by default
docs.html:
0006. Use the cloud's managed agent runtime by default

  • Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-16

Context

Agents need session state, scaling, isolation, identity and tracing. We can build that on Kubernetes or use Vertex AI Agent Engine (Google Cloud) or Bedrock AgentCore Runtime (AWS).

Decision

Run agents on the managed runtime by default. Use GKE or EKS only for agents with unusual networking, throughput or framework needs. Build agents with frameworks that run on both (ADK, Strands or others), and keep tool access on MCP and delegation on A2A, so the choice stays reversible per agent.

Consequences

  • Less platform code to own; faster start.
  • Feature availability varies by region and changes quickly; validate during design.
  • Some vendor coupling at the runtime layer, contained by open protocols at the seams.

Alternatives considered

Option Why not
Self-host everything on Kubernetes More undifferentiated work; slower to production.
